title: Introduction to ASP.NET Core MVC
description: Learn what ASP.NET Core MVC is, its history, features, architecture, and how it compares to older .NET web frameworks.

data.text: **ASP.NET Core MVC** is Microsoft's open-source, cross-platform framework for building modern web applications. It is built on the **Model-View-Controller (MVC)** architectural pattern and combines the best ideas from Agile Development and the broader .NET ecosystem. If you want to build structured, testable, and high-performance websites with C#, ASP.NET Core MVC is the framework to learn.
A Brief History of ASP.NET Core

Microsoft released the first version of **ASP.NET Core** in 2016. It was a ground-up rewrite of the older ASP.NET framework, designed from scratch to be cross-platform, fast, and modular. The current stable release at the time of this course is **.NET 8.0**, which continues this tradition of yearly improvements.
ASP.NET Core vs. ASP.NET Web Forms
Before ASP.NET Core, Microsoft offered **ASP.NET Web Forms** — a drag-and-drop, event-driven model popular in the early 2000s. Here is how the two compare:

data.text: Key Features of ASP.NET Core MVC

terms.definition: Build and run on Windows, Linux, and macOS using the same codebase.
A built-in system for supplying classes with their dependencies, making apps loosely coupled and easy to test.
A chain of request-processing components that can handle authentication, routing, logging, and more.
Server-side attributes that enrich standard HTML elements with server-side behavior, e.g. asp-for, asp-action.
Maps incoming URL patterns to controller action methods, enabling clean, SEO-friendly URLs.
Automatically maps HTTP request data (form fields, query strings, route values) to C# model objects.

data.title: Feature Highlights
items: **Open Source** — the full source code is on GitHub at [github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore).
**Cross-Platform** — develop on any OS using Visual Studio, VS Code, or any editor.
**Full HTML Control** — write raw HTML, CSS, and JavaScript without the abstraction of server controls.
**Full HTTP Control** — work directly with HTTP requests and responses, making AJAX and SPAs easy.
**Extensible** — plug in View Components, Tag Helpers, custom routing, and third-party libraries.
**Testable** — the separation of Models, Views, and Controllers makes unit and integration testing straightforward.
**Client-Side Integration** — use jQuery, React, Angular, Bootstrap, or any frontend framework side by side.

data.text: SEO-Friendly URLs Through Routing

ASP.NET Core's routing engine turns meaningful URL patterns into controller actions. Instead of `Product.aspx?id=42`, you get `/products/shoes/42` — a URL that search engines and humans can both read easily.

data.text: What Is the MVC Architecture?
**Model-View-Controller (MVC)** is a design pattern that separates an application into three interconnected parts. Each part has a single, clear responsibility.

data.caption: The MVC request lifecycle: the browser sends a request to the Controller, which reads/writes the Model and selects a View.
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    Browser["Browser Request
(e.g. /Employees)"] --> Controller
    Controller["Controller
(fetch data, apply logic)"]
    Controller -->|reads & writes| Model["Model
(data + business rules)"]
    Controller -->|selects| View["View
(HTML rendered to browser)"]
    View -->|HTML Response| Browser

data.text: Model

The **Model** holds your application's data and business rules. It is typically a C# class with properties (e.g. `Employee { string Name; int Age; }`). Models know nothing about the browser or HTML. They communicate only with Controllers.
View

The **View** is the user interface. It is an HTML template (Razor `.cshtml` file) that renders data passed to it by the Controller. Views contain no business logic and communicate only with Controllers — never directly with Models.
Controller

The **Controller** is the traffic cop. It receives every HTTP request, runs any necessary logic, loads or updates the Model, and selects a View to render. A single ASP.NET Core MVC app can have dozens of controllers, each with many action methods.

data.title: A Minimal Controller
data.content: A controller action that passes a Model to a View.

data.title: Remember the Separation
data.text: Models never talk to Views directly. Controllers never render HTML themselves — they always delegate to a View. Keeping these boundaries clean is what makes MVC apps maintainable at scale.
Installing Visual Studio 2022 or VS Code
You can use either Visual Studio 2022 or VS Code for this course. Both work equally well.

data.title: Visual Studio 2022 Community
items: Free for individual developers, students, and open-source contributors.
Windows and macOS supported (macOS has fewer features).
During installation, select the **ASP.NET and web development** workload.

data.title: Visual Studio Code
items: Completely free, open-source, and runs on all operating systems.
After installing VS Code, install the **C# Dev Kit** extension from the Extensions marketplace.
The extension provides IntelliSense, debugging, and project management for .NET.

data.text: The .NET Version You Should Use

This course uses **.NET 8.0**, which is a Long-Term Support (LTS) release. LTS versions receive security updates and patches for three years, making them the safest choice for production apps. Newer versions like .NET 9.0 exist but are Standard-Term Support (STS) releases.

data.expectedOutcome: You can trace a URL from the browser through the Controller to the Model and back as an HTML View.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: ASP.NET Core MVC is Microsoft's modern, cross-platform web framework built on the MVC pattern.
It replaced older ASP.NET Web Forms and legacy ASP.NET MVC with a lighter, faster, and testable architecture.
The MVC pattern cleanly separates data (Model), UI (View), and request handling (Controller).
Routing turns friendly URLs into controller actions automatically.
Visual Studio 2022 and VS Code are both fully supported — pick the one that fits your OS and workflow.
data.takeaway: You now understand what ASP.NET Core MVC is and how its architecture works. Next, you will build your first application from scratch.
